item.title: ABOUT
item.dc:creator: MikulasKarpeta
item.content:encoded:
PHOTOGRAPHER, ARTIST

Elera Vance

I am a portrait photographer who has spent fifteen years studying faces. I've shot Fortune 500 executives, household names, and the occasional head of state — each time looking for the same thing: the moment they forget there's a camera in the room. That's when the real portrait begins.

The Eyes Behind
the Lens

Based in London and Paris, Elara Vance is a contemporary photographer whose work explores the intersection of architectural minimalism and human emotion. With a career spanning over a decade, she has developed a signature style characterized by stark compositions, a muted tonal palette, and an unflinching focus on the subject's essence.

After graduating from the Royal College of Art, Elara began her journey documenting the evolving urban landscapes of Europe. Her transition into fashion and portraiture allowed her to bring that same structural discipline to the human form, resulting in images that feel both grounded and ethereal. Her approach is rooted in patience—waiting for that precise nanosecond where the light, the environment, and the emotion converge.

COMMON INQUIRIES

I work across portrait commissions — from corporate headshots and executive sessions to editorial work and celebrity shoots. If there's a face worth photographing and a client who's serious about the result, I'm interested.

Every session starts with a brief call to understand what you need from the images and how they'll be used. On the day, I handle everything — lighting, direction, atmosphere. After, I deliver retouched selects within a week, usually less.

Both. The brief has to be interesting and the client has to care about the result. I've shot heads of state and first-time founders. What matters is that the image does something useful — not just that it exists.

A corporate headshot session can be booked within two weeks. Editorial and advertising commissions need more lead time — typically three to four weeks for planning and scheduling. I don't rush the preparation, which is why the shoots themselves always run smoothly.

Mostly: an honest brief and the confidence to let me run the session. Tell me who's being photographed, what the images are for, and what you want them to communicate. The rest I'll handle. Bringing examples of images you admire also helps — not to copy them, but to understand your instincts.

item.title: People of Prague
item.dc:creator: MikulasKarpeta
item.content:encoded:
STREET PHOTO

People of Prague

I came to Prague in November, when the tourist crowds thin and the city settles back into itself, and I spent my mornings at tram stops, bakeries, and the edges of local markets. I chose to shoot on medium format film, which slowed me down deliberately — each frame cost something, so I only pressed the shutter when I was certain. The cold light of Central European autumn gave every portrait a quiet, interior quality that I hadn't planned for but came to love. Prague gave me people who were guarded at first and generous once they understood what I was trying to do.

item.title: Still Here
item.dc:creator: MikulasKarpeta
item.content:encoded:
STUDIO

Still Here

This series began as an experiment in stripping everything away — no location, no story, no context beyond what a person carries in their face. I worked with a single large softbox and a seamless white background, keeping the setup identical for every session so that the only variable was the subject. Each sitting lasted about two hours, long enough for the initial self-consciousness to dissolve and something more unguarded to come through. What I was looking for, and what I think I found in some of these frames, is the expression that exists in the space between poses — unheld, unperformed.

item.title: People of Tbilisi
item.dc:creator: MikulasKarpeta
item.content:encoded:
STREET PHOTO

People of Tbilisi

Walking through Tbilisi's tangled old town, I spent three weeks approaching strangers in courtyards, markets, and tea houses, asking if I could photograph them where they stood. I worked entirely with natural light — the city's golden afternoon sun and the deep shadow of its narrow balconied streets became my studio. Most of my subjects spoke no English and I spoke no Georgian, so everything was communicated through gesture, patience, and the moment someone finally relaxed and forgot about the camera. What emerged was a portrait of a city that feels both ancient and restless, carried in the faces of the people who call it home.
